slides.title: Part 1 — Meaning as geometry
slides.body: Tokens are arbitrary integers — token 12 has no relationship to token 13. Embeddings fix that by giving every token a *location in space*, arranged so that **distance encodes meaning**. This space is the substrate every later layer manipulates.

slides.title: Words become vectors
slides.body:
An **embedding** is a learned vector for each token. Picture a room where every word has a position: `dog` sits near `cat` (both pets), `king` near `queen` (royalty), `Paris` near `France` (geography).

Explore the space on the right — notice that semantically related words cluster. A real transformer embedding has 768–4096 dimensions, but the geometric intuition (near = related) holds in any dimension.

The model is never *told* that dog and cat are similar. That structure **emerges** from training.

slides.title: Similarity is direction (cosine), not length
slides.body:
"How related are two words?" usually means **cosine similarity** — the cosine of the angle between their vectors:

$$\cos(\theta) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert\,\lVert v\rVert}$$

- Same direction → cosine ≈ 1 (very related).
- Perpendicular → 0 (unrelated).
- Opposite → -1 (anti-related).

Magnitude is largely ignored for semantics (vectors are often L2-normalized). What matters is *which way* a vector points. This is the exact quantity attention will compute between queries and keys — so this geometry is not optional background, it is the mechanism.

slides.title: Why this geometry appears: distributional training
slides.body:
Embeddings are **learned**, not designed. In a transformer the embedding layer is one matrix $E$ of shape $[\text{vocab},\, d_{model}]$; token id 42 simply fetches row 42. Gradients from next-token prediction flow back into $E$ and nudge rows.

The **distributional hypothesis**: words in similar contexts get similar vectors. `king` and `queen` co-occur with *royal, throne, crown*, so training pulls their rows together. Trained on hundreds of billions of tokens, the famous analogy structure $\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman} \approx \text{queen}$ (Mikolov et al., 2013) emerges as a side effect.

question.question: Which pair would you expect to have the HIGHEST cosine similarity in a well-trained embedding space?
question.explanation: doctor and nurse share contexts (hospital, patient, medicine), so training drives their vectors into similar directions. The other pairs share little contextual structure, so their angles stay large (low cosine).

question.question: Two embedding vectors point the same direction but one is 10× longer. Their cosine similarity is:
options: ≈ 1 — cosine divides out magnitude, so only direction matters
Undefined for vectors of different length
question.explanation: Cosine normalizes by both magnitudes (‖u‖‖v‖), so a pure scaling cancels out: same direction ⇒ cosine ≈ 1 regardless of length. This is exactly why semantic similarity is an angle, not a distance.

slides.title: Part 3 — Embeddings inside the transformer
slides.body: Embeddings are the *start*, not the destination. Everything downstream is a transformation of this vector field.

slides.title: Tied weights and the output head
slides.body:
Many transformers **tie** the input embedding matrix to the output projection: the same $E$ that turned tokens into vectors is reused (transposed) at the end to turn the final vector back into vocabulary logits. This shares parameters and tends to improve quality.

So the embedding matrix is doing double duty — encoding meaning on the way in *and* scoring tokens on the way out. A subtle consequence: improving how a token is represented also improves how confidently it can be predicted.

slides.title: Contextual vs static
slides.body:
The embedding-table vector is **static** — `bank` gets one vector whether it's a river bank or a money bank. The transformer's job is to make representations **contextual**: each attention layer mixes in information from surrounding tokens so that, by the upper layers, `bank` in *"river bank"* and *"savings bank"* have moved to different places.

That's the bridge to the rest of the path: the static embedding is the raw material; attention is the machine that contextualizes it.

question.question: In a transformer, where does the meaning of the WORD 'bank' get disambiguated between 'river bank' and 'savings bank'?
options: In the attention layers, which mix in surrounding-token information to make the representation contextual
In the embedding table — it stores both senses
In the tokenizer, which splits the two senses
It is never disambiguated; the model guesses
question.explanation: The embedding table is static (one vector per token id). Disambiguation happens because attention layers blend in context (river vs savings), moving the token's representation toward the right sense as it flows up the stack.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body:
- An **embedding** places each token in a learned vector space where **direction encodes meaning** (cosine similarity).
- The structure is **learned** from context (distributional hypothesis), not designed.
- The embedding matrix is often **tied** to the output head.
- Table embeddings are **static**; attention makes them **contextual**.

**Next:** [Positional encoding](/wiki/positional-encoding) — injecting word *order* into these vectors — then [attention](/wiki/attention), which computes the dot-product geometry you just learned.
